q-140479.name: Question 1
q-140479.problem:
Which of the following sets are orthogonal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$
q-140479.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0,\,{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0,\,{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=-3+0-2+2=-3\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=4-4=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+0-4+2=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+6-4-2=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2+4=8\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ only".

  1. U={[10−22],[−3111]}
  2. V={[10−22],[03−2−2],[2221]}

  • u1⋅u2=0.

  • v1⋅v2=0,v1⋅v3=0,v2⋅v3=0.

  • w1⋅w2=0.

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

  • For the set U, we get the following: u1⋅u2=[10−22]⋅[−3111]=−3+0−2+2=−3≠0× So, U is not an orthogonal set.

  • For the set V, we get the following: v1⋅v2=[10−22]⋅[03−2−2]=4−4=0✓v1⋅v3=[10−22]⋅[2221]=2+0−4+2=0✓v2⋅v3=[03−2−2]⋅[2221]=0+6−4−2=0✓ So, the set V is orthogonal.

  • For the set W, notice that w1⋅w2=[1−14]⋅[2−21]=2+2+4=8≠0× So, W is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "V only".

q-40288.name: Question 2
q-40288.problem:
Which of the following sets are orthogonal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}15 \\ -20\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}$
q-40288.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2},{w}_{3}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,\,{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\,{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0.$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0.$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0,\,{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0,\,{w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- The set $U$ cannot be orthogonal since it contains  $3$ vectors from ${R}^{2}$ (in which we can have an orthogonal set with at most 2 non-zero vectors). Therefore, $U$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=0+10=10\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $W,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=12+3-1=14\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "None of the listed".

q-82399.name: Question 3
q-82399.problem:
Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\}$
q-82399.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0 \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=0 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1 \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=0+12+6=18\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{12}{25}-\frac{12}{25}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only".

q-81109.problem:

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{13}+\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}+7{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4 & 7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{26}{5} & \frac{38}{5} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1} & ={x}_{3}-2(\frac{19}{13}{x}_{3}) \\ 5{x}_{1} & =-\frac{25}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1} & =-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{13}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{19}{13}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=13$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 19 \\ 13\end{aligned}].

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 19 \\ 13\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=-\frac{5}{19}.$

q-83768.problem:
Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$
q-83768.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} & -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{6}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{21}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(-2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{14}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{21}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}|+|-\frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}|=\frac{6}{\sqrt{14}}.$

$$
